rendered: The authors did not run the separation step at room temperature by design. The Cyrene-based separation is run hot, because PVDF precipitates out of Cyrene when the mixture is cool.[1] At room temperature the PVDF/Cyrene mixture becomes very viscous and gels: its viscosity is far higher than at the elevated temperature, and an organogel forms at a higher PVDF loading.[2] Room-temperature filtration was tested as a comparison. PVDF stayed on the separated powder, showing that it reprecipitated onto the cathode particles on cooling, whereas hot filtration removed it.[3] PVDF dissolves in Cyrene only above a threshold temperature of about ~90 °C[4], so the separation has to be kept above that temperature.[5] Room temperature does appear once, in the recovery step: the hot supernatant is cooled to room temperature so that PVDF and carbon black phase-separate and can be filtered off, together with the recycled Cyrene.[6]
